relationship: Historical narrative parallel: Israel flees on Mount Gelboue
rationale: Both accounts open the final battle with the foreigners fighting Israel, Israel fleeing, and wounded men falling on Mount Gelboue.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: Saul’s three sons struck
rationale: Both accounts place the deaths of Saul’s named sons in the foreigners’ pursuit of Saul and his sons; each account retains its own forms of the sons’ names.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: archers find Saul
rationale: Both describe the battle weighing heavily on Saul and archers finding him. Chronicles describes his suffering from the bows, while Samuel specifies a wound beneath the ribs.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: Saul falls on his sword
rationale: Both give Saul’s request to his equipment bearer, the bearer’s fearful refusal, and Saul’s falling on his own sword to avoid the foreigners’ abuse.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: the equipment bearer’s death
rationale: Both report the bearer seeing that Saul was dead and then falling on his own sword and dying.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel with distinct scope: deaths on the same day
rationale: Both summarize Saul and his three sons dying together that day. Chronicles adds all his house, while Samuel expressly includes the armour-bearer; their stated groups are preserved.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: abandoned cities occupied
rationale: Both connect the Israelites’ flight from their cities with news that Saul and his sons were dead, and then report the foreigners occupying those cities.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: bodies found the next day
rationale: Both report the foreigners coming to strip the fallen on the following day and finding Saul and his sons on Gelboue.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: equipment and announced victory
rationale: Both describe Saul being stripped and news being sent throughout the foreigners’ land to their idols and people. Chronicles additionally mentions taking his head.

relationship: Historical narrative contrast: trophies displayed after Saul’s death
rationale: Both describe the victorious foreigners dedicating Saul’s equipment in a divine house. Chronicles places his head in Dagon’s house; Samuel names Astarte’s temple and Saul’s body on Beth-shan’s wall, retaining the different objects and locations.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: news reaches the rescuers
rationale: Both introduce the response to Saul’s mistreatment through the inhabitants hearing what the foreigners had done; Chronicles names those dwelling in Galaad, while Samuel specifies Jabesh in Gilead.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel with distinct burial details: recovery and mourning
rationale: Both describe mighty men recovering Saul’s body and a son’s or sons’ bodies, taking the remains to Jabis or Jabesh, burying bones, and fasting seven days. Chronicles gives an oak; Samuel includes burning and describes cultivated ground, so the burial descriptions remain distinct.

relationship: Narrative explanation: Saul consults the medium and hears Samuel
rationale: Chronicles’ judgment expressly mentions Saul’s inquiry through a medium and Samuel’s answer. Samuel narrates Saul requesting the medium, asking for Samuel, and hearing judgment for disobedience.

relationship: Judgment announcement and retrospective outcome: David receives the kingdom
rationale: Samuel announces that the Lord will give Saul’s kingdom to David and deliver Saul and his sons to death; Chronicles retrospectively attributes Saul’s death and the transfer to David to the Lord.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: Israel’s kinship appeal at Hebron
rationale: Both introduce Israel’s coming to David at Hebron with the people’s declaration that they are his bones and flesh.

relationship: Historical speech parallel: David will shepherd Israel
rationale: Both speeches recall David leading Israel during Saul’s reign and quote the Lord’s appointment of David to shepherd and rule His people.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: covenant and anointing at Hebron
rationale: Both report Israel’s elders coming to Hebron, David making a covenant before the Lord, and his anointing over Israel. Chronicles additionally ties this to the Lord’s word through Samuel.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: advance against Jerusalem’s Jebusites
rationale: Both place David and his men at Jerusalem, confronting its Jebusite inhabitants; Chronicles also supplies the name Jebus.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: refusal followed by capture of Zion
rationale: Both give resistance to David entering Jerusalem and then report his capture of Zion, identified as the City of David. Samuel has additional words about the blind and lame.

relationship: Historical narrative comparison: David’s challenge against the Jebusites
rationale: Both accounts include David’s declaration about striking a Jebusite during Jerusalem’s capture. Chronicles specifies leadership as the reward and Joab’s success; Samuel records a differently worded command without that appointment.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: David settles in the stronghold
rationale: Both report David settling in the captured fortified place and connect it with the name City of David.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: building the captured city
rationale: Both describe David building the city around after taking and settling its fortified place. Chronicles also mentions fighting and taking the city.

relationship: Repeated royal assessment: the Lord accompanies David’s growth
rationale: Both state that David grew greater and that the Lord Almighty was with him, expressly relating his expanding power to divine presence.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative connection: David’s supporters and Israel’s anointing
rationale: The mighty-men heading says they strengthened David’s kingdom together with all Israel according to the Lord’s word; the earlier Hebron notice narrates Israel’s elders covenanting with and anointing him according to that word.

relationship: Warrior-list parallel with distinct totals: the opening exploit
rationale: Both warrior lists begin with a leading warrior’s single assault against many. Chronicles records Jesebaal and three hundred wounded, while Samuel’s opening entry records eight hundred slain; neither names nor totals are equated.

relationship: Warrior-list parallel: Eleazar among the three
rationale: Both lists introduce Eleazar after the opening warrior and place him among the three mighty men. The descriptions of his parentage and affiliation are retained as each passage gives them.

relationship: Battle-scene parallel with distinct participants and crops: the defended field
rationale: Both scenes describe foreigners gathering near a cultivated plot and the people fleeing. Chronicles has barley in the account following Eleazar, while Samuel introduces Shammah and lentils; the participants and crops are not combined.

relationship: Battle-scene parallel: a plot defended and deliverance from the Lord
rationale: Both describe a warrior standing in the middle of the plot, saving it, striking the foreigners, and the Lord bringing great deliverance. The link compares the narrated deed without identifying the differently introduced warriors.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: three approach David at the cave
rationale: Both describe three of the thirty coming down to David at a cave while foreigners camp in the valley; each passage retains its own cave and valley name forms.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: David’s refuge and Bethlehem’s garrison
rationale: Both set David in a fortified enclosure while the foreigners maintain a garrison or outpost in Bethlehem, establishing the danger behind the water request.

relationship: Historical speech parallel: David desires Bethlehem’s water
rationale: Both quote David longing for drinking water from the Bethlehem cistern by the gate.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: dangerous water becomes an offering
rationale: Both describe the three breaking through the foreigners, drawing the requested water, bringing it to David, and David refusing to drink and pouring it out to the Lord.

relationship: Historical speech parallel: water likened to the men’s blood
rationale: Both explain David’s refusal through his question about drinking the blood of men who risked their lives and conclude that these were deeds of the three.

relationship: Warrior-list parallel with distinct weapons: Joab’s brother
rationale: Both entries describe Joab’s brother leading the three, an exploit against three hundred, and his renown among them. Chronicles has a sword and wounded men; Samuel has a spear and slain men.

relationship: Warrior-list parallel: command and the limit of rank
rationale: Both entries give the preceding warrior honor and command but explicitly say he did not attain to the three; Chronicles additionally states honor above the two.

relationship: Warrior-deed parallel: Moabite opponents and a lion in snow
rationale: Both accounts describe the warrior’s deeds against two Moabite opponents and a lion in a pit or cistern on a snowy day. Chronicles says two ariels; Samuel says two sons of Ariel, preserving the distinct objects.

relationship: Warrior-deed parallel: an Egyptian killed with his own spear
rationale: Both describe a conspicuous Egyptian holding a large spear, the warrior approaching with a staff, taking the spear, and killing the Egyptian with it. Chronicles additionally gives the Egyptian’s five-cubit height.

relationship: Warrior-list parallel: renown after the recorded deeds
rationale: Both close the warrior’s exploit account by crediting the preceding deeds and stating his name among the three mighty men, with each passage’s personal name forms retained.

relationship: Warrior-list comparison with distinct rank and appointment wording
rationale: Both conclude with honor, a statement that the warrior did not attain to the three, and David’s appointment. Chronicles says honor above the thirty and appointment over his ancestral house; Samuel says renowned among the three and appointed to receive instructions.

relationship: Warrior-list parallel: Joab’s brother and a Bethlehem warrior
rationale: Both roster openings name Joab’s brother and a second warrior linked to Dodo or Dodi and Bethlehem, while retaining their different personal name forms and Samuel’s explicit membership among the thirty.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Sammoth and Chelles among David’s warriors
rationale: Sammoth and Chelles continue the list introduced as the mighty men of the forces; the heading supplies their place in David’s warrior roster without identifying them with differently named men elsewhere.

relationship: Warrior-roster parallel: the Tekoite family description and Abiezer
rationale: Both roster passages include a Tekoite described through an Ekkes or Ikkesh father-name and Abiezer the Anathothite. The link retains the two rosters’ wording rather than resolving their variant name forms.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Sobochai and Eli among the forces
rationale: The names Sobochai the Asothite and Eli the Achoite continue the roster governed by the heading mighty men of the forces, rather than supplying an otherwise unrecorded deed for them.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: the Netophathite entries
rationale: Moorai and Cholod son of Nooza are listed as Netophathites within the mighty-men roster opened by the target heading, which supplies the military role of this otherwise bare name line.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Aithi and Banaias in the mighty-men list
rationale: Aithi son of Ribai and Banaias the Pharathonite continue the list introduced as the mighty men of the forces. The heading establishes their roster role without equating similar names in other lists.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Ouri and Abiel among the mighty men
rationale: Ouri from Nachaligaas and Abiel the Garabeththite occur within the continuing roster introduced by the target heading; their listed origins are preserved without adding a narrative exploit.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Azmoth and Eliaba in David’s forces
rationale: The bare names Azmoth and Eliaba belong grammatically to the target’s mighty-men roster, which supplies the role under which these two locality descriptions are recorded.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Bennaias, Osom, and Jonathan
rationale: The three names continue the mighty men of the forces list introduced by the heading. The connection preserves the source’s separate names and Jonathan’s stated father without reconstructing another roster.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Achim and Elphal as listed warriors
rationale: Achim son of Sachar and Elphal son of Our occur under the mighty-men-of-the-forces heading. This supplies their stated military setting without inferring identities from similar names elsewhere.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Ophar and Achia as listed warriors
rationale: The line naming Ophar the Mochorathite and Achia the Phelonite continues the roster opened by mighty men of the forces; the link identifies the literary role of the line’s two names.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Eserai and Naarai as listed warriors
rationale: Eserai and Naarai son of Azobai continue the target heading’s roster of the mighty men of the forces, providing a concrete classification for this otherwise unexplained name line.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Joel and Mebaar as listed warriors
rationale: Joel, identified as Nathan’s brother, and Mebaar son of Agari belong to the continuing mighty-men roster introduced in the target. Their different family descriptions remain exactly as given.

relationship: Warrior-roster parallel: an Ammonite and Joab’s equipment bearer
rationale: Both lists place an Ammonite beside a man described as bearing Joab’s equipment. The personal and family name forms differ between the lists, so this compares the paired descriptions without equating every name.

relationship: Warrior-roster parallel: Ira and Gareb
rationale: Both rosters pair Ira and Gareb with the same shared affiliation within each list; Chronicles gives Jetherite and Samuel gives Ithrite, retaining those source forms.

relationship: Warrior-roster parallel: Uriah’s entry
rationale: Both mighty-men lists contain Uriah with an ethnic designation, Chettite in Chronicles and Hittite in Samuel. Chronicles continues with Zabet, while Samuel closes with its own total of thirty-seven.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Adina’s Reubenite command
rationale: Adina of Reuben, explicitly called a ruler with thirty alongside him, appears in the continuing mighty-men roster introduced by the target heading; his thirty are not substituted for another list’s total.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Anan and Josaphat among the mighty men
rationale: Anan son of Moocha and Josaphat the Baithanite continue the named list governed by the heading mighty men of the forces, identifying their recorded role without invented exploits.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Ozia and Chothan’s sons
rationale: Ozia, Samma, and Jiiel continue the mighty-men roster. The target heading supplies their role, while the source expressly groups Samma and Jiiel as sons of Chothan.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Jediel and his brother Joazae
rationale: Jediel son of Sameri and Joazae his brother continue the mighty men of the forces list. Their explicit brother relationship is preserved within that military roster.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: the penultimate warrior entries
rationale: Eliel, Jaribi and his son Josia, Elnaam, and Jethema the Moabite are recorded within the continuing mighty-men list introduced by the target, preserving its stated father-son grouping and affiliation.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: the list’s closing names
rationale: Aliel, Obed, and Jesiel the Misabite close the roster introduced as the mighty men of the forces, making the heading the explicit literary explanation of this final name line.

relationship: Narrative setting: David receives a country town while away from Saul
rationale: Chronicles introduces helpers joining David at Soklag while he was kept from Saul; Samuel narrates Achish granting David the country town Ziklag. Each passage’s place form is retained.

relationship: Same-chapter grammatical connection: the helpers’ weapons and origin
rationale: The description of bows, slings, and Benjaminite kinship continues the men introduced as coming to David at Soklag and helping him in war; the target supplies the subject and setting of this descriptive line.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: the opening Benjaminite helpers
rationale: Achiezer and the following named men begin the roster governed by the opening description of men helping David at Soklag, with right- and left-handed weapons and origin among Saul’s Benjaminite brethren.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Samaias among David’s helpers
rationale: Samaias the Gabaonite continues the list introduced as Benjaminite helpers at Soklag. The source adds his specific distinction among and over the thirty, beyond the heading’s general military description.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Jermias through Jozabad
rationale: The line naming Jermias, Jeziel, Joanan, and Jozabad continues the opening roster of men who came to David at Soklag to help in war; their role follows from that explicit introduction.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Eliazai through Saphatia
rationale: These five names continue the roster introduced as David’s military helpers at Soklag from Saul’s Benjaminite brethren, supplying the setting and stated role for the otherwise bare names.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: the Korite entries
rationale: Elkana, Jesouni, Ozriel, Joazar, and Jesboam are listed within the opening helpers roster. The target gives the Soklag setting and military role; their Korite description is preserved without a further ancestry claim.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: Iraam’s sons close the first list
rationale: Elia and Zabadia, expressly called sons of Iraam and sons of Gedor, finish the opening list of helpers who came to David at Soklag before the following Gadite group is introduced.

relationship: Same-chapter heading and summary: the Gadite military group
rationale: The introduction describes Gaddites joining David with shields, spears, strength, and speed; the subsequent summary expressly calls the listed men Gad’s sons and rulers of the army.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: the first three Gadite leaders
rationale: Azer, Abdia, and Eliab begin the numbered list following the introduction of Gaddite warriors who separated themselves to David; the heading supplies the group and military setting of their ranks.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: the fourth and fifth Gadite leaders
rationale: Masemanne and Jermia continue the numbered list under the introduction of Gaddite warriors joining David, retaining their stated fourth and fifth positions.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: the sixth and seventh Gadite leaders
rationale: Eththi and Eliab continue the numbered roster governed by the Gaddite-warrior introduction, which supplies the group and military setting for their sixth and seventh ranks.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: the eighth and ninth Gadite leaders
rationale: Joanan and Eliazer continue the numbered roster of Gaddites who came to David from the wilderness, preserving their respective eighth and ninth positions.

relationship: Same-chapter roster grammar: the tenth and eleventh Gadite leaders
rationale: Jermia and Machabannai complete the numbered list introduced as Gaddite warriors joining David, giving the concrete group to which these final two ranked names belong.

relationship: Same-chapter summary and heading: Gad’s army rulers
rationale: The summary identifies the preceding named men as Gad’s sons and army rulers; the opening heading describes the same listed group coming to David with martial strength and equipment.

relationship: Narrative circumstance parallel: crossing the overflowing Jordan
rationale: Both accounts explicitly place a Jordan crossing when the river overflowed its banks. Joshua narrates priests, stopped water, and dry ground; Chronicles attributes a crossing and the routing of valley inhabitants to the preceding warriors without claiming that miracle.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative connection: arrivals tested and received
rationale: Benjaminite and Judahite men come to help David; the following encounter records his test of their peaceful intent, Amasai’s assurance, and David receiving them as force leaders.

relationship: Same-chapter speech and response: David’s test of peaceful intent
rationale: David asks whether the newcomers come in peace or to betray him; Amasai answers with repeated peace and divine help, and David receives them and appoints them leaders.

relationship: Same-chapter response to a stated test: Amasai’s peace assurance
rationale: Amasai’s declaration of peace and God’s help answers David’s preceding demand to know whether the arrivals are peaceful helpers or agents of his enemies; David’s reception follows that assurance.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: the generals refuse David’s help
rationale: Both accounts give the foreigners’ generals’ fear that David could regain Saul’s favor with their men’s heads, explaining his exclusion from their war. Chronicles additionally introduces Manassites joining him.

relationship: Same-chapter roster and occasion: the named Manassite leaders
rationale: The named leaders of Manasseh’s thousands elaborate the preceding statement that some from Manasseh came over to David during his exclusion from the foreigners’ campaign; this line locates their joining on his journey to Soklag.

relationship: Narrative campaign connection with bounded identification: David and the geddour
rationale: Chronicles says the newly listed men fought alongside David against the Geddour; Samuel describes David inquiring about pursuit of a geddour and setting out with his men. Samuel does not name these Manassite leaders, so their individual participation is not supplied from that passage.

relationship: Same-chapter literary development: helpers become a great force
rationale: The chapter opens with men coming to David as helpers in war; the later summary explicitly describes daily arrivals forming a great force, developing that same movement of military support.

relationship: Same-chapter heading and concluding summary: support for David at Hebron
rationale: The army heading says the men came to Hebron to transfer Saul’s kingdom to David according to the Lord’s word; the concluding summary repeats Hebron, David’s reign, and Israel’s united purpose.

relationship: Same-chapter contingent and stated purpose: Judah’s armed men
rationale: Judah’s six thousand eight hundred shield- and spear-bearing men begin the contingent list introduced as the army leaders coming to Hebron to transfer Saul’s kingdom to David; the total is a listed contingent rather than all Judah.

relationship: Same-chapter contingent and stated purpose: Simeon’s warriors
rationale: Simeon’s seven thousand one hundred battle-ready men continue the list governed by the Hebron assembly heading, which supplies their stated purpose in transferring Saul’s kingdom to David.

relationship: Same-chapter contingent and stated purpose: Levi’s men
rationale: The four thousand six hundred from Levi are listed under the heading of forces coming to David at Hebron for the kingdom’s transfer, without converting this contingent into a census of all Levites.

relationship: Same-chapter contingent and stated purpose: Joadae’s Aaronite leadership
rationale: Joadae, called leader for Aaron with three thousand seven hundred alongside him, occurs in the army list introduced as coming to Hebron to transfer Saul’s kingdom to David; the heading establishes the occasion for his leadership.

relationship: Same-chapter contingent and stated purpose: Sadok and his ancestral rulers
rationale: Sadok and the twenty-two rulers from his ancestral house continue the forces listed under the Hebron transfer-of-kingship heading. His youthful strength and the twenty-two rulers remain the source’s specific description.

relationship: Same-chapter contingent with qualified allegiance: Benjamin’s men
rationale: The three thousand Benjaminites are listed among those coming to Hebron for David’s kingship, while this entry expressly adds that most still guarded Saul’s house; the qualification is retained rather than erased by the heading.

relationship: Same-chapter contingent and stated purpose: Ephraim’s men of renown
rationale: Ephraim’s twenty thousand eight hundred mighty men continue the Hebron army list whose heading states the transfer of Saul’s kingdom to David; the entry’s ancestral-house renown describes this particular contingent.

relationship: Same-chapter contingent and concluding purpose: Manasseh’s designated men
rationale: The eighteen thousand from half Manasseh are explicitly designated for David to reign; the closing summary gives the same purpose for the assembled warriors and Israel’s united support.

relationship: Same-chapter contingent and stated occasion: Issachar’s discerning leaders
rationale: Issachar’s two hundred leaders and their brethren continue the list of those coming to David at Hebron. Their discernment concerns what Israel should do in relation to leadership, within that stated royal assembly.

relationship: Same-chapter contingent and concluding unity: Zaboulon’s support
rationale: Zaboulon’s fifty thousand are expressly described as helping David without leaning another way; the chapter’s conclusion likewise describes the gathered warriors and Israel as united for David’s reign.

relationship: Same-chapter contingent and stated purpose: Nephthali’s armed group
rationale: Nephthali’s one thousand rulers and thirty-seven thousand shield- and spear-bearers continue the army list introduced as coming to Hebron for David’s kingship, preserving the separate counts of rulers and armed companions.

relationship: Same-chapter contingent and stated purpose: the Danites
rationale: The twenty-eight thousand eight hundred Danites arrayed for war are one contingent under the heading of forces coming to Hebron to transfer Saul’s kingdom to David.

relationship: Same-chapter contingent and stated purpose: Aser’s helpers
rationale: Aser’s forty thousand going out to help in war continue the forces listed under the heading of coming to David at Hebron for the transfer of kingship, supplying the occasion for this contingent’s aid.

relationship: Same-chapter contingent and stated purpose: forces from beyond Jordan
rationale: The one hundred twenty thousand from Reuben, Gaddi, and half Manasseh complete the armed contingent list introduced by the Hebron kingship-transfer heading; the source’s combined total remains attached to these named groups.

relationship: Historical narrative connection: Israel unites for David’s kingship
rationale: Chronicles summarizes the warriors and Israel’s shared purpose for David to reign at Hebron; Samuel narrates Israel’s tribes and elders coming there, making a covenant, and anointing him over all Israel.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative connection: the Hebron gathering shares food
rationale: The men’s three days of eating and drinking follow the explicit gathering at Hebron for David’s reign; the preceding summary identifies the warriors and united Israel whose assembly this hospitality serves.

relationship: Same-chapter provision and celebration: food for the assembly
rationale: The detailed food deliveries from neighboring groups explain and extend the preceding statement that the brethren had prepared food for the three-day gathering; the source expressly connects the abundance with gladness in Israel.

relationship: Same-chapter consultation and agreed proposal: assembling for the ark
rationale: David’s consultation with military leaders leads into his proposal to the whole assembly to gather Israel with priests and Levites and bring the ark; the people then agree to the stated course.

relationship: Same-chapter proposal and acceptance: gathering Israel
rationale: David proposes sending to the remaining brethren and the priests and Levites to gather; the assembly’s following agreement is the explicit response to this proposal and the ark transfer it introduces.

relationship: Narrative intention and later assembly: bringing the ark
rationale: David proposes transferring God’s ark to the people; the later passage describes his assembling all Israel at Jerusalem to bring it to the prepared place. The later assembly follows the intervening interruption rather than making the first attempt successful.

relationship: Same-chapter assent and its content: David’s ark proposal
rationale: The whole assembly’s agreement refers directly to David’s preceding proposal to gather the brethren with priests and Levites and transfer God’s ark, supplying the concrete matter approved.

relationship: Historical narrative comparison: Israel gathered to bring the ark
rationale: Both accounts describe David gathering Israel and setting out to bring God’s ark. Chronicles gives the assembly’s geographical extent and Jarim; Samuel gives about seventy thousand young men and an ascent from Judah’s rulers, retaining the different descriptions.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel with distinct route wording: the cherubim-enthroned Lord
rationale: Both ark-journey accounts describe the ark through the Lord’s name and His enthronement upon cherubim. Chronicles gives its own City of David and Judah wording; Samuel speaks of an ascent from Judah’s rulers, without those route descriptions being reconciled.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: ark transported on a new cart
rationale: Both describe the ark placed on a new cart from Amminadab’s or Abinadab’s house and driven by Oza or Uzzah with his brethren; the source name forms and Samuel’s added family details are preserved.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: David and Israel celebrate before the ark
rationale: Both describe David and Israel celebrating with strength, songs, lyres, harps, tambourines, and cymbals. Chronicles additionally names trumpets where Samuel names pipes, preserving the different instrument lists.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: reaching to steady the ark
rationale: Both describe the party reaching a threshing floor and Oza or Uzzah stretching out his hand to hold the ark because of a calf’s movement. Chronicles says the calf tipped it; Samuel gives the fuller pulling-aside description.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel with stated cause: death beside the ark
rationale: Both describe the Lord’s anger, His striking Oza or Uzzah, and death there before God. Chronicles explicitly attaches the judgment to stretching his hand upon the ark, retaining that stated cause.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: David’s distress and the place name
rationale: Both describe David’s disheartenment over the Lord’s action against the man and derive the place’s continuing name from that action; each retains its own Cutting or Breach wording and personal name form.

relationship: Historical speech parallel: David fears receiving the ark
rationale: Both report David’s fear that day and quote his question about how God’s ark could come to him, connecting the death with his hesitation about the journey.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: ark diverted to another house
rationale: Both report David declining to bring the ark to himself in the City of David and turning it aside to a Geththite or Gittite householder, retaining Abeddara and Obed-edom as the passages give them.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: three months and household blessing
rationale: Both record the ark remaining in the house for three months and God blessing the householder and all that was his; Chronicles’ Abeddara and Abeddaram forms remain distinct from Samuel’s Obed-edom.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: Tyre supplies David’s house builders
rationale: Both describe Tyre’s king sending David messengers, cedar, and skilled builders for a house; Chronicles gives Chiram and Samuel Hiram, with each account’s builder descriptions preserved.

relationship: Repeated royal assessment: David established for Israel’s sake
rationale: Both report David recognizing the Lord’s establishment of his kingship and its exaltation for the sake of Israel, explicitly explaining the kingdom’s growth in relation to the people.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: David’s growing Jerusalem household
rationale: Both report David taking more wives at Jerusalem and having additional sons and daughters there. Samuel also mentions concubines and the move from Hebron; those details are additional to Chronicles’ statement.

relationship: Repeated family roster with distinct name forms: Jerusalem’s first four sons
rationale: Both lists introduce sons born in Jerusalem and list four names ending with Nathan and Solomon. Chapter 14 gives Samaa and Isobaam, while chapter 3 gives Samaa and Sobab and supplies their mother; the forms and additional genealogy are preserved.

relationship: Repeated family-roster position with distinct middle name
rationale: Both Jerusalem-son lists place Ibaar and Eliphalet in this three-name line. Chapter 14’s middle name is Elisae, while chapter 3 has Elisama, so the shared roster position does not erase the difference.

relationship: Repeated family roster: Nage, Naphag, and the third son
rationale: Both Jerusalem-son lists place Nage and Naphag together with a third name, Janouou here and Janoue in chapter 3; the passage forms are retained without an independent name derivation.

relationship: Repeated family-roster ending with distinct name forms
rationale: Both Jerusalem-son lists end this sequence with Eliphalet after two other names. Chapter 14 gives Elisamae and Balegdae, while chapter 3 gives Elisama and Eliada; the parallel placement is recorded without equating the differing forms.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel with distinct response: foreigners seek David
rationale: Both say the foreigners heard David had been anointed king over Israel and went up to seek him. Chronicles says David went out to meet them, while Samuel says he went down to the stronghold.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel with distinct valley designation
rationale: Both place the foreigners in the valley before David’s inquiry. Chronicles calls it the Valley of the Giants and says they fell upon it; Samuel calls it the Valley of the Titans and says they gathered there.

relationship: Historical speech parallel: David asks whether to attack
rationale: Both quote David asking whether to go up against the foreigners and whether God will give them into his hands, followed by the Lord’s command to go and promise of victory.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel with distinct site forms: water-like breakthrough
rationale: Both report David striking the foreigners and explaining the victory through a water-like divine breakthrough that yields the place’s name. Chronicles gives Baalpharasin and Cutting of Pharasin; Samuel gives Upper Breaches, without reconciling those forms.

relationship: Legal command and later royal command: burn the foreign gods
rationale: The law commands burning the gods’ graven images with fire; Chronicles reports David ordering the abandoned gods burned. The connection concerns the stated commands and does not change David’s order into an explicit report of its execution.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: the foreigners return to the valley
rationale: Both describe another advance by the foreigners into the valley after the first defeat, retaining Chronicles’ Valley of the Giants and Samuel’s Valley of the Titans designations.

relationship: Historical speech parallel with distinct approach wording: a changed tactic
rationale: Both record David asking God again and receiving instructions to turn away rather than make the earlier approach. Chronicles directs approach near pear trees; Samuel speaks of the place of weeping, preserving the distinct directions and site wording.

relationship: Historical speech parallel: sound signals the Lord’s advance
rationale: Both commands make a heard sound the signal to attack because the Lord goes before David to strike the foreigners. Chronicles describes shaking in pear-tree tops, while Samuel describes the grove of weeping closing together.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: obedience and the extent of victory
rationale: Both report David doing as God commanded and striking the foreigners along a route from Gabaon or Gibeon to Gazara or the land of Gezer, retaining the passages’ different geographical forms.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative result: God-given victory and David’s renown
rationale: The closing notice attributes the nations’ fear of David to the Lord; the preceding inquiry and victory expressly give the enemies into David’s hands and attribute the breakthrough to God, explaining the narrated basis for his growing reputation.
